5	Answer semantics:
6	- hypothesis: "supported" = the evidence, taken together, supports the claim more than its rivals; "contradicted" = the evidence counts against it; "unknown" = the evidence does not discriminate, so the claim is live but unestablished.
7	- edge (a claimed link from one condition to another): "causal" = the evidence supports a causal link (for example temporal order plus mechanism plus covariation with the main rival ruled out, a natural experiment, or an intervention result); "association-only" = they co-occur or correlate in the evidence but causation is not established; "contradicted" = evidence counts against the link; "unknown" = evidence is insufficient even to show association.
8	- action: "preferred" = among the best next actions given the evidence; "acceptable" = reasonable but not among the best; "premature" = could be right if a still-unconfirmed hypothesis were confirmed, but committing now is not justified; "harmful" = likely to worsen outcomes, suppress information, punish the wrong party, or disable a protective control.
9	- sufficiency (item SUFF): is the evidence sufficient to commit to the action you rank highest, where that action is substantive rather than merely evidence-gathering? "sufficient" or "insufficient". Concluding that no intervention is warranted counts as a substantive decision.
10	- Items with asOfStage set must be answered using only evidence whose stage is at or before that stage.

228	CASE OD2-DEV2-INTERACT: Larkfield DC: robot collision stops tripled in September
229	
230	Setting: Larkfield Distribution Centre is a fictional regional warehouse run by Corrin Freight Logistics. It operates 58 Halvane HR-7 autonomous mobile robots. Thirty-eight pallet-handling robots work the outbound marshalling Zones A and B, where wrapped outbound pallets are staged. Twenty tote robots work carton Zone C. A robot logs a 'collision stop' (protective stop) whenever an obstacle enters its protective field. The analysis date is 20 October 2026.
231	
232	Presenting request: The regional operations director writes: 'Larkfield's robot collision stops have roughly tripled since early September, in the middle of peak season. The GM wants a disciplinary policy for agency temps, and Halvane suggests shortening the robots' protective fields. Tell me what is actually driving the stops and what the site should do now.'
233	
234	INITIAL EVIDENCE
235	E1 [stage S1] Fleet management system, weekly safety KPI extract (system-record): Larkfield DC: protective ('collision') stops, all 58 HR-7 robots, by ISO week 2026: wk30 201, wk31 209, wk32 198, wk33 212, wk34 207, wk35 203, wk36 412, wk37 640, wk38 655, wk39 662, wk40 648, wk41 651. A stop is logged whenever an obstacle enters a robot's protective field; the robot halts until the field clears, typically for 20–90 seconds. Physical contacts with people or equipment: 1 in weeks 30–35, 1 in weeks 37–41. Robot operating hours were roughly constant across the period.
236	E2 [stage S1] Email from Dana Okafor, General Manager, to site leadership, 5 October (leadership-account): Subject: Robot stops. 'The timing tells the story. We brought in 46 agency temps on 31 August and the stops tripled that same week. These people don't know the lane rules and they wander into robot aisles. I want a three-strike policy live by Monday. Every collision stop gets matched to the temps rostered in that zone during that hour, each match counts as a strike, and after three strikes the agency replaces the person. Engineering keeps telling me it's the software, but Halvane says their update runs fine at other sites, so let's stop chasing that.'
237	E3 [stage S1] Change record CHG-2026-0412 (change-record): Fleet firmware upgrade, HR-7 6.3 to 6.4. Implemented 2–4 September 2026 on 50 of 58 robots. Exception: eight pallet-handling robots with the older battery module (units P31–P38) stay on 6.3 until a compatible module arrives. They continue in normal mixed duty. Vendor release summary: 'Revised near-field return filtering for improved detection of low-profile obstacles; navigation and charging fixes; security patches.' Halvane lifecycle notice: security support for 6.3 ends 31 October 2026. The eight exception units are covered by a time-limited waiver.
238	E4 [stage S1] Email from Halvane Robotics Customer Support (Tier 2), 25 September (vendor-account): 'We've reviewed your ticket. Firmware 6.4 has been live at three other customer sites since July with no change in protective-stop rates, so we don't see the firmware as the cause. Increases like this are usually environmental: people, layout, clutter. If the stops are hurting throughput, a common remedy is to shorten the protective field by 20%, and we can push that profile to your fleet remotely. Our next release, 6.4.2, is planned for early December and includes further filtering refinements.'
239	E5 [stage S1] Interview notes, R. Szabo, robot maintenance technician, 12 October (staff-account): 'Most of the stops I get called out to are in the marshalling lanes, A and B, where outbound pallets are staged. There are hardly any in C, the tote zone. Usually by the time I get there the field's clear and nobody's around, but people walk off, so I can't say who it was. Somebody asked me about the new shiny pallet wrap; procurement switched suppliers at the start of August. I don't buy it. We had that wrap for a month before the stops went up and nothing changed. If it was the wrap, August would have been bad too.'
240	E6 [stage S1] Outbound performance dashboard, weeks 30–41 (system-record): Missed carrier cut-offs averaged 2 per week in weeks 30–35 and 9 per week in weeks 37–41. Outbound pallet volume has been up 18% since week 35 as the seasonal peak ramped. Comparison row for the same weeks in 2025: cut-off misses rose from 2 to 7 per week during that peak, while collision stops stayed near 200 per week. Dashboard note: robot stop time is not linked to wave completion data.
241	
242	EVIDENCE CATALOGUE (collect at most 3; read the file path to collect)
243	X1 [stage S1] Warehouse lighting work orders, January–October - source: Facilities management system (change-record) - file: evidence/X1.txt
244	X2 [stage S1] Bench test of protective stops against staged outbound pallets, 14 October - source: Test record co-signed by site engineering lead and Halvane field engineer (document) - file: evidence/X2.txt
245	X3 [stage S1] Procurement record for the outbound stretch film change, July–August - source: Procurement system (financial-record) - file: evidence/X3.txt
246	X4 [stage S1] Wave-level analysis of missed carrier cut-offs, weeks 37–41 - source: Outbound planning analyst (document) - file: evidence/X4.txt
247	X5 [stage S1] Site safety committee minutes, 8 October - source: Safety committee secretary (document) - file: evidence/X5.txt
248	X6 [stage S1] Halvane statement on 6.4 stop rates at other customer sites - source: Halvane Robotics account manager (vendor-account) - file: evidence/X6.txt
249	X7 [stage S1] Agency temp induction and safety-training records, August–September - source: HR and staffing agency records (document) - file: evidence/X7.txt
250	X8 [stage S1] Wi-Fi access-point and fleet-server latency logs, weeks 30–41 - source: IT network monitoring (log) - file: evidence/X8.txt
251	X9 [stage S1] Stretch film technical data sheets, current and previous supplier - source: Packaging suppliers' published specifications (document) - file: evidence/X9.txt
252	X10 [stage S1] Robot-related near-miss and contact incident reports, weeks 30–41 - source: Site safety reporting system (system-record) - file: evidence/X10.txt
253	X11 [stage S1] Lidar window cleaning and calibration log, July–October - source: Maintenance management system (log) - file: evidence/X11.txt
254	X12 [stage S1] Robot battery health telemetry, July–October - source: Fleet management system (telemetry) - file: evidence/X12.txt
255	X13 [stage S1] Collision-stop event log with badge-tag proximity field, weeks 30–41 - source: Fleet management system export with HR roster note (log) - file: evidence/X13.txt
256	X14 [stage S1] Collision-stop rates by firmware group and zone, weeks 33–41 - source: Site engineering analysis of fleet telemetry (telemetry) - file: evidence/X14.txt
257	X15 [stage S1] Fleet configuration and map change history, July–October - source: Fleet manager audit trail (change-record) - file: evidence/X15.txt
258	
259	CANDIDATE HYPOTHESES
260	H1: The September fleet firmware update, on its own, caused the rise in collision stops.
261	H2: The August change of outbound pallet stretch film, on its own, caused the rise in collision stops.
262	H3: Seasonal agency temps entering robot lanes caused the rise in collision stops.
263	H4: The September firmware update and the August film change together caused the rise in collision stops; neither would have produced it alone.
264	H5: The September firmware update and the arrival of the agency temps together caused the rise in collision stops; neither would have produced it alone.
265	H6: Halvane's planned December release would, on its own, bring stop rates back to the pre-September level while the current film stays in use.
266	
267	CANDIDATE CAUSAL LINKS
268	R1: Fleet firmware update from 6.3 to 6.4 (2–4 September) -> Tripling of weekly collision stops (contributes to)
269	R2: Switch to the new outbound stretch film (August) -> Tripling of weekly collision stops (contributes to)
270	R3: Arrival of 46 agency temps on the floor (31 August) -> Tripling of weekly collision stops (contributes to)
271	R4: Tripling of weekly collision stops -> Rise in missed carrier cut-offs (contributes to)
272	
273	CANDIDATE ACTIONS
274	A1: Switch outbound pallets back to the previous supplier's stretch film, keep all robots on their current firmware, and track weekly stop rates by zone and firmware group against the September–October figures.
275	A2: Roll the 30 upgraded pallet-handling robots back to firmware 6.3 under a temporary waiver until Halvane issues a corrected release, leaving the tote robots on 6.4.
276	A3: Accept Halvane's offer to shorten the protective field by 20% on all robots to cut stop frequency during peak.
277	A4: Introduce the GM's three-strike policy: match each collision stop to temps rostered in that zone and hour, and have the agency replace any temp who reaches three strikes.
278	A5: Keep the current film and adopt Halvane's planned December release as the permanent fix, scheduling fleet-wide installation as soon as it ships.
279

282	S02: hypothesis H2 allowed=[supported, contradicted, unknown]
283	S03: hypothesis H3 allowed=[supported, contradicted, unknown]
284	S04: hypothesis H4 allowed=[supported, contradicted, unknown]
285	S05: hypothesis H5 allowed=[supported, contradicted, unknown]
286	S06: hypothesis H6 allowed=[supported, contradicted, unknown]

288	S08: edge R2 allowed=[causal, association-only, contradicted, unknown]
289	S09: edge R3 allowed=[causal, association-only, contradicted, unknown]
290	S10: edge R4 allowed=[causal, association-only, contradicted, unknown]
291	S11: action A1 allowed=[preferred, acceptable, premature, harmful]
292	S12: action A2 allowed=[preferred, acceptable, premature, harmful]

# EDF Specification v0.3

Status: Working draft

This is the authoritative EDF v0.3 specification for the current draft.

Under EDF's constitutional version integrity rule, this defines a subsequent version rather than changing the meaning of v0.2 retroactively.

EDF evolves under constitutional rules defined in [constitution.md](constitution.md). The constitution governs framework evolution, not how to perform an EDF analysis.

## Purpose

EDF is a systems understanding framework with a diagnostic grammar.

It is used to explain how a system produced an outcome and to identify the highest-leverage opportunities for influencing future outcomes.

EDF is not primarily a decision framework. It establishes confidence in reality before decision frameworks such as Clarity evaluate what to do next.

Diagnostic Calibration is an optional extension for comparing, challenging, refining, and synthesizing multiple EDF analyses of the same system.

Framework changes should remain consistent with the constitutional rules of EDF.

## Design Rule

If a new concept does not improve one of the five verbs, it does not belong in EDF.

The five verbs are:

- Define
- Observe
- Explain
- Influence
- Validate

## Context Principle

Every EDF analysis is valid only within its declared System Context.

## Required Diagnostic Sequence

Every EDF analysis should follow this sequence:

1. Define the System Context
   - Primary System
   - Context
   - Focus
2. Define the Outcome
3. Identify Manifestation(s)
4. Build the Origin Network
5. Trace Propagation
6. Evaluate Evidence
7. Identify Control Points
8. Rank Control Points
9. Determine Diagnostic Sufficiency

## Sequence Notes

### 1. Define the System Context

Every EDF begins by declaring its System Context.

System Context has three required fields:

- Primary System
- Context
- Focus

These define what is being analyzed, what larger system materially influences it, and what aspect of the primary system is under examination.

Different analyses may disagree partly because they declared different System Contexts. That is not automatically a conflict in evidence.

### 2. Define the Outcome

State the outcome in factual terms, not interpretive terms.

Good:

- Two aircraft were lost and the fleet was grounded
- The mission landed on the moon and returned safely

Weak:

- Management failed
- The launch culture was broken

### 3. Identify Manifestation(s)

Manifestations are observable signals.

They are how the outcome appears in the world. A complex outcome may have several manifestations.

### 4. Build the Origin Network

Identify the contributing origins that made the outcome possible.

Origins may be:

- Technical
- Human
- Organizational
- Environmental
- Financial
- Regulatory

Complex outcomes should usually be modeled as an origin network rather than a single root cause.

### 5. Trace Propagation

Describe how effects moved from the origin network to the manifestations and outcome.

Propagation paths may be:

- Physical
- Informational
- Organizational
- Financial
- Human

### 6. Evaluate Evidence

Separate direct observation from inference.

Evaluate the quality of evidence supporting the current model and note meaningful gaps or disputes.

### 7. Identify Control Points

Identify where intervention could most effectively influence future outcomes.

Control points may differ from origins.

### 8. Rank Control Points

Rank candidate control points using:

- Influence
- Controllability
- Cost
- Confidence

The ranking does not need false precision. It does need a defensible ordering.

### 9. Determine Diagnostic Sufficiency

Ask:

> Do we understand enough to take the next responsible action?

Diagnosis is sufficient when additional investigation is unlikely to materially change the next responsible action.

## Required Output Elements

All EDF outputs should include, at minimum:

- System Context
- Primary System
- Context
- Focus
- Outcome
- Manifestation(s)
- Origin Network
- Propagation
- Evidence
- Control Points
- Control Point Ranking
- Confidence
- Diagnostic Sufficiency
- Unknowns
- Next Responsible Action

## Optional Extension: Diagnostic Calibration

Diagnostic Calibration is not required for routine EDF use.

Use it when:

- The situation is complex
- The stakes are high
- Causes are disputed
- Multiple disciplines are involved
- The cost of being wrong is significant

Diagnostic Calibration uses multiple independent EDF analyses to improve confidence in the diagnostic model while preserving valuable disciplinary perspectives.

See [diagnostic-calibration.md](diagnostic-calibration.md).

## Relationship To Complexity Levels

- Use [EDF-0](complexity-levels.md#edf-0-rapid) for rapid, low-complexity situations.
- Use [EDF-1](complexity-levels.md#edf-1-standard) when evidence and alternatives matter.
- Use [EDF-2](complexity-levels.md#edf-2-complex) when multiple interacting origins and layered control points must be modeled.

The sequence remains the same across levels. The depth changes.

## Relationship To Clarity

EDF creates the diagnostic grammar.

Diagnostic Calibration improves confidence in the diagnostic model.

Clarity uses the calibrated understanding to evaluate decisions.

## Additional decision rules for this analysis

1. Treat the presenting request as one hypothesis, not a fact. Keep its rivals live until evidence rules them out: no real problem (normal variation or a baseline explains it); an intentional tradeoff; an outside cause; a measurement or reporting artifact; a cause in a different unit or component from the one blamed.
2. Judge every action by what it would do under every live hypothesis, not only the leading one. An action is harmful if it is likely to cause damage even when the leading hypothesis is true: punishing the messenger or the wrong party, suppressing information, rewarding a gamed metric, or disabling a protective control. An action is premature if it is only sensible when a still-unconfirmed hypothesis is true.
3. "No intervention is warranted" is a valid, sufficient conclusion when the evidence shows the problem does not exist or is an accepted tradeoff.
4. Evidence collection is governed by value of information. Before each collection, name the live hypotheses and the answer or action that is most uncertain. Collect an item only if its title suggests it could discriminate between live hypotheses or change your next action. Stop as soon as no remaining item could change your next action. The collection limit is a hard constraint; never exceed it, even for evidence you believe is decisive.

Setting: Larkfield Distribution Centre is a fictional regional warehouse run by Corrin Freight Logistics. It operates 58 Halvane HR-7 autonomous mobile robots. Thirty-eight pallet-handling robots work the outbound marshalling Zones A and B, where wrapped outbound pallets are staged. Twenty tote robots work carton Zone C. Presenting request: The regional operations director writes: 'Larkfield's robot collision stops have roughly tripled since early September, in the middle of peak season. input.brief: The tripling of stops comes from the firmware 6.4 upgrade interacting with the new gloss stretch film. It isn't caused by the temps. Firmware 6.4 keeps weak short-range returns that 6.3 discarded, and the gloss film on staged pallets produces such returns at oblique angles. A bench test with no people present showed 17/20 stops for 6.4 with gloss film. The other three combinations gave 1/20, 0/20 and 0/20. Fleet data agrees. Upgraded pallet robots in Zones A/B rose from 3.2 to 15.6 stops per 100 robot-hours, while the 6.3 robots working the same zones stayed flat at about 3.1 to 3.3. Tote robots in Zone C, where no wrapped pallets are staged, were unchanged. Nearly all the added stops had no person nearby, and temps were spread across all zones. I am fairly confident (about 85%). Next steps: switch back to the previous matte film, which restores normal rates without a firmware change, and track stops weekly by zone and firmware group. Roll the 30 pallet robots back to 6.3 only if the film can't be changed quickly. Don't adopt the three-strike policy or the shortened protective fields, because they would punish the wrong people and weaken safety. Test the December release against the gloss film before relying on it.
